P01.note: Singular possessive: one lone geologist made the sketches. A (plural possessive) attracts through 'survey teams' and 'Researchers'.
P01.not_hard_because: 'a lone geologist' in the first sentence hands over the number, and 'sketches' right after the blank makes the two non-possessive forms obviously wrong.

P02.note: Singular subject 'a diner' takes 'judges'; the pronoun refers to the one oddly precise price, confirmed by singular 'figure'. B attracts via 'several rounded prices'.
P02.not_hard_because: 'a diner typically' sits directly before the blank and gives the verb number away; 'the more carefully calculated figure' (singular) then settles the pronoun.

P03.note: Plural subject needed for plural verb 'record'; D attracts by misreading 'record' as a noun after a possessive.
P03.not_hard_because: the bare plural verb 'record' immediately after the blank settles it, and 'several youths' already signals plural; same noun-plus-'record(s)' template as P34.

P04.not_hard_because: plural 'tenants' sits directly before the blank so the two singular options die on sight, and 'stays'/'publishes' hand over the present tense.

P05.note: Introductory clause 'As the crew blasted the ridge' takes its object and then a comma before the main subject 'the water level'. A is a garden path (intransitive 'blasted') that strands 'the ridge'.
P05.not_hard_because: the standard introductory-clause comma; reading on to 'the water level ... began' exposes A and B at once, and P21 uses the same object-or-subject boundary.

P06.convention: restrictive participle: 'those letters written to the copyist' can pick out the copyist letters within the bundle, since the passage never says every letter in the bundle went to the copyist
P06.note: With only one bundle surviving, 'those letters' is already identified and the participle reads as nonessential (A). But 'those ... written to' is a natural restrictive demonstrative, so B can also be defended.
P06.not_hard_because: 'Only one bundle' in the first sentence is the same count cue that decides P13 the other way, and D's trailing comma is garbled; but fix the exclusivity first: B is defensible.

P07.note: Singular 'curtain' takes 'was'; 'them' refers to the stagehands. B attracts with 'it' (the auditorium).
P07.not_hard_because: 'curtain' sits right before the blank and gives the number away, and the only plausible agent, 'the stagehands', is plural; the same 2x2 verb-plus-pronoun grid recurs in seven other items.

P08.note: The town had exactly one newspaper, so the name is a nonrestrictive appositive; the dash sets it off through the end of the sentence. A (restrictive) attracts because names often follow without punctuation.
P08.not_hard_because: 'exactly one newspaper' in the first sentence hands over the nonrestrictive reading, and D ('the,') is a pattern nobody picks.

P09.note: Plural possessive: seven growers pool one harvest. A (singular possessive) and B (plain plural) are the attractors.
P09.not_hard_because: 'Seven small apple growers' opens the passage and gives the number away; same count-cue possessive template as P01.

P10.note: Singular 'bell' plus a closed past event ('on the day of the count's funeral').
P10.not_hard_because: no plural attractor ('town' next to the blank is singular too), and 'on the day of the count's funeral' hands over the past tense.

P11.note: Mass-noun subject 'Bilingualism' is singular; 'during the harbor's first expansion' is a closed past time, which rules out A's present perfect. B attracts through 'vendors' after the blank.
P11.not_hard_because: singular 'Bilingualism' directly before the blank, and 'during the harbor's first expansion' gives away simple past over A.

P12.note: The list items carry internal commas ('a narrow-angle camera, the heaviest instrument aboard'), so they are separated by semicolons, matching 'path; and'.
P12.not_hard_because: the semicolon printed later ('flight path; and') is simply copied into the parallel slot.

P13.note: With three lots, 'gathered during an unusually dry summer' identifies which lot, so it is restrictive and takes no punctuation. B and C set it off as nonessential.
P13.not_hard_because: 'three separate lots' in the first sentence hands over the restrictive reading; it mirrors P06 with the count flipped, and D's trailing comma is garbled.

P14.note: Nonrestrictive appositive 'the widow of the shop's first foreman' closed by the comma already printed after 'foreman'. B (colon) is the most attractive alternative.
P14.not_hard_because: the comma after 'foreman' is already printed, so the key just opens the pair.

P15.note: 'Each' is singular; 'when the sponsor replaced' sets the past progressive. A attracts through 'volunteers' and 'sites'.
P15.not_hard_because: 'Each of' is the textbook singular cue and 'when the sponsor replaced' hands over the tense.

P16.note: 'The illiterate' (the + adjective, meaning illiterate people) is plural, and 'since' requires the present perfect, so 'have been'. B is the strong trap because the subject has no plural ending.

P17.note: The colon introduces an independent clause ('the ring ... matched a seal') that names the ignored detail. A is a comma splice once the verb 'matched' is found past the embedded appositive.
P17.not_hard_because: D ('the,') is garbled, and once 'matched' is found A and B are a plain splice and run-on; same template as P24 and P25.

P18.note: Plural 'parasites' takes 'are removed'; agent 'them' = the wrasses. The singular 'grouper' next to the blank attracts A and C.
P18.not_hard_because: the 'by it' options have no sensible antecedent, so once the head noun 'parasites' is found the item is settled; same 2x2 grid as P07.

P19.note: Plural 'teams' takes 'have'; the wording belongs to the questionnaire, so 'its'. 'province' next to the blank attracts 'has', and C's 'their' attracts through 'teams'.
P19.not_hard_because: the two halves are independent binary choices from the same 2x2 grid as seven other items, and 'its wording' points back to 'questionnaire' in the same clause.

P20.note: Singular 'editor' takes 'was'; the novel ('its closing scene') is the thing revised, so 'it'. D attracts through 'sonnets' and 'letters'.
P20.not_hard_because: 'its closing scene' right after the blank settles the pronoun as singular, which is the same number as the verb, so one decision gives both.

P21.note: Garden path: 'spray' must be intransitive so that 'the vines growing along the lowest terraces' can be the main subject of 'were showing'. A and B read 'the vines' as the object and leave 'were showing' with no subject.

P22.note: Plural 'engineers' takes 'have'; the reconstructed thing is the single 'closing burst of telemetry', so 'it'. A attracts through 'partial copies' after the blank.
P22.not_hard_because: 'engineers' sits right before the blank and gives the verb away; same 2x2 grid as P07.

P23.note: Plural 'copyists' plus 'when raiders set fire' (an action interrupted in the past) gives 'were decorating'. C (present perfect) and B ('monastery' attractor) are the distractors.
P23.not_hard_because: 'when raiders set fire' hands over the past progressive, and the plural head 'copyists' is only three words from the blank.

P24.note: Two independent clauses ('showed a faint gray line' / 'the crack ... ran the full depth'). The semicolon is right; the colon fails because the second clause reports a later event rather than explaining the first. The unpunctuated modifier 'no wider than a strand of hair and invisible from the walkway above' needs commas, which makes the second clause hard to read; this is a quality defect.
P24.not_hard_because: A is a splice and B a run-on as soon as 'ran' is found; the semicolon-or-colon choice is the only real decision, and the template repeats P17 and P25.

P25.note: 'The tough cord twisted from ... goats' is the subject of 'also strung', so a new sentence starts. B is a strong garden path that reads it as an appositive to 'catgut'; D attracts as an explanation colon, but the second clause adds a fact rather than explaining.

P26.note: Singular 'restorer' plus 'before the council halted' gives the past progressive 'was cleaning'. D attracts through 'paintings' next to the blank.
P26.not_hard_because: 'before the council halted' hands over the past tense, leaving only number, and the subject 'the restorer' starts the clause.

P27.note: Singular 'study' plus 'since the housing-market crash' gives 'has been following'. B attracts through 'interns' next to the blank.
P27.not_hard_because: 'since' hands over the present perfect, the same cue as P35 and P36.

P28.note: Pro-verb ellipsis: 'do' stands in for 'lengthen', picked up only later from 'barely lengthens'. The subject is plural 'tapes', and 'were' has nothing to substitute for. D tempts because 'nineteenth-century' suggests the past.

P29.note: Singular 'ending' takes 'has ... vanished' across the interrupting phrase. B attracts through 'verbs', and A ('is vanished') is archaic.
P29.not_hard_because: once 'vanished' is found the auxiliary must be 'has/have', and the head 'ending' is singular; same separated-auxiliary template as P30.

P30.note: Plural 'trees' plus 'susceptible' (an adjective, so 'have seldom susceptible' lacks 'been') plus the past survey gives 'were seldom'.
P30.not_hard_because: once 'susceptible' is found the 'has/have' options are ungrammatical, and 'trees' is plainly plural.

P31.note: Plural 'plates' plus 'while the brickwork overhead cooled' gives the past progressive passive. C and D attract through 'furnace' and 'wall'.
P31.not_hard_because: 'cooled' in the while-clause hands over the tense, and 'plates' heads the subject.

P32.note: Singular 'pancreas' (despite the -s) plus generic present ('unless the animals receive'). A attracts through 'mice'.
P32.not_hard_because: 'unless the animals receive' hands over the present tense, leaving only the -s noun trap, which a strong student knows.

P33.note: Singular 'receiver' takes 'is'; 'them' refers to the meteoroids. 'domes' attracts the plural verb, and 'it' attracts through 'receiver'.
P33.not_hard_because: the same 2x2 verb-plus-pronoun grid as seven other items; 'receiver' is singular and the only trackable plural is 'meteoroids'.

P34.note: Exactly one clerk, so singular subject 'clerk' with the verb 'records'. C attracts by reading 'records' as a noun.
P34.not_hard_because: 'exactly one clerk' in the first sentence plus the verb 'records' right after the blank; this is the same template as P03.

P35.note: Plural 'tutors' plus 'since the closure' gives 'have coached'. C attracts through 'branch'.
P35.not_hard_because: 'since' hands over the present perfect (same as P27 and P36), and 'tutors' heads the subject.

P36.note: Singular 'ointment' plus 'since the network rewrote' gives 'has been prescribed'. C attracts through the fronted 'clinics'.
P36.not_hard_because: 'since' again hands over the present perfect (P27, P35), and 'ointment' sits right before the blank.

P37.note: Singular 'face' plus generic present ('whenever ... reaches') gives 'is prone'. B attracts through 'crevasses' and 'glaciologists'.
P37.not_hard_because: 'face' sits directly before the blank and 'reaches' hands over the present tense.

P38.note: Plural 'copes' plus 'during the siege' gives past 'were removed'.
P38.not_hard_because: plural 'copes' sits next to the blank with no attractor, and 'during the siege' gives away the past tense.

P39.note: Plural 'technicians' takes 'are'; 'their' refers to the young animals' or technicians' transmitters. D attracts through 'an adult'.
P39.not_hard_because: plural 'technicians' sits right before the blank and the plural 'young animals' gives the pronoun; same 2x2 grid as the others.

P40.note: Plural 'segments' plus 'on the last night of ... shutdown' (a closed past time) gives 'were cleaned'. C attracts through 'mirror's'.
P40.not_hard_because: the closed past time phrase hands over the tense, and 'segments' is plural and close to the blank.

tells: A first-sentence count ('a lone geologist', 'several youths', 'exactly one newspaper', 'Seven small apple growers', 'three separate lots', 'Only one bundle', 'exactly one clerk') hands over the number or the restrictiveness in P01, P03, P06, P08, P09, P13 and P34, so test-takers learn to read the first sentence for a count.
Options of the shape 'word the,' or 'word word,' with a trailing comma (P06 D, P08 D, P13 D, P17 D) always lose; the exception is P05 D, which is the key.
Eight items (P02, P07, P18, P19, P20, P22, P33, P39) use the same 2x2 verb-number by pronoun-number grid; an option whose pronoun has no sensible antecedent always loses.

In every tense item the time cue is explicit and decisive: 'since' always means present perfect (P16, P27, P35, P36), and a closed past phrase always means simple or progressive past (P10, P11, P23, P26, P31, P38, P40).
near_duplicates: plural or singular noun before a 'record(s)' verb that reads as a possessive noun
possessive number given by a first-sentence count
restrictive vs nonrestrictive participle decided by a first-sentence count
introductory clause comma at the object-or-subject boundary garden path
independent-clause boundary before a heavily modified subject
2x2 verb number by pronoun number grid
'since' present perfect with a plural or singular attractor
past agreement with a closed time phrase and a nearby attractor
auxiliary separated from its participle or complement by a long phrase
generic present singular head with a plural attractor
